title: Defects of kind and defects of degree
source_text: XVII. Defectus prioris generis specificus est & essentialis & actionem aliqua essentiali perfectione privat. Sed posterioris generis defectus gradualis est & accidentalis & ab actione tollit perfectionem tantum accidentalem & individualem. Adeoque actus ille cui aliquid priori modo deest, ita malus est ut simpliciter bonus dici non possit: si vero solum posteriori modo ipsi aliquid desit, non desinit esse vere & proprie bonus, licet imperfectam tantum bonitatem habeat.
pass_a_gloss: XVII. A defect of the former kind is specific & essential & deprives the action of some essential perfection. But a defect of the latter kind is gradual & accidental & takes from the action only an accidental & individual perfection. And so that act to which something is lacking in the former way, is so bad that it cannot be called simply good: but if something is lacking to it only in the latter way, it does not cease to be truly & properly good, although it has only an imperfect goodness.
pass_b_english: Thesis XVII. A defect of the first kind concerns the act's kind and essence, and robs it of some essential perfection. A defect of the second kind is one of degree and is accidental: it removes from the act only an accidental, individual perfection.

So an act that lacks something in the first way is bad, so bad that it cannot be called good without qualification. An act that lacks something only in the second way does not stop being truly and properly good, though its goodness is imperfect.

lemmas.gloss: is a gradual and accidental defect

lemmas.latin: non desinit esse vere & proprie bonus
lemmas.gloss: does not cease to be truly and properly good

choices.why: The scholastic distinction between a defect of kind, which makes an act bad, and a defect of degree, which leaves it good but imperfect.
